---
title: "An assessment pipeline from blueprint to bank monitoring"
description: >
  Take a certification exam through every stage of the mirtverse assessment
  pipeline, with the checks and decisions at each step.
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", warning = FALSE)
```

A test passes through many hands before a score reaches a test taker: a
blueprint, item writing, review, a field test, calibration, form assembly,
standard setting, scoring, security checks, a report and, after each
administration, a look at the health of the item bank. The **assessment
pipeline** in mirtverse puts these steps in one object. Each stage does its
work, then runs a *gate*: a set of checks that records what it finds as
**flags** for you to consider before the next stage.

This article takes the `certexam` data (a simulated 32-item certification exam
taken by 1,200 candidates in English or French) through every stage. The data
have problems planted in them, and the gates find them.

```{r}
library(mirtverse)
```

## The pipeline object and its rules

```{r}
p <- mv_pipeline("Certification exam")
p
```

Every check compares a statistic with a threshold from `mv_rules()`. The
defaults follow common operational practice and every one can be changed by
name, for example `mv_rules(q3 = 0.25)`, or relaxed for a pilot study with
`mv_rules(preset = "lenient")`.

Flags have three levels:

- **info**: for awareness.
- **review**: something a psychometrician should look at.
- **block**: a problem that makes later stages unsafe.

By default flags only warn, so every stage still runs. With
`mv_pipeline(strict = TRUE)`, a stage refuses to start while an earlier stage
has open review or block flags.

## 0. Blueprint

The blueprint is the contract that later stages check against: what the test
measures, how scores will be used, and how many items each content area
needs on a form.

```{r}
p <- set_blueprint(p, c(Ethics = 4, Practice = 5, Law = 3),
                   construct = "Professional knowledge for certification",
                   use = "pass/fail certification", reliability = 0.85)
p$blueprint$cells
```

Because the score supports a pass/fail decision, we asked for a reliability
of at least 0.85. That target replaces the default `reliability` rule, so the
calibration gate will hold the test to it.

## 1–2. Item writing and review

`generate_items()` drafts multiple-choice and open-ended items for each
blueprint cell with a language model through the ellmer package. It checks
the drafts (a second model call verifies each key) and flags disputed keys,
weak distractors, near-duplicate items and readability above the grade level.
Items written by people come in with `add_items()` and pass the same checks.

`review_packet()` writes a spreadsheet for content and sensitivity
reviewers, optionally with an AI screen. `read_reviews()` reads their
decisions back and flags items without enough reviewers, items judged
misaligned or biased, and low agreement between reviewers.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
p <- generate_items(p, n = 3)            # needs an API key for the model provider
p <- review_packet(p, "review.xlsx", reviewers = c("Ana", "Ben", "Chen"))
p <- read_reviews(p, "review-returned.xlsx")
```

The certexam items already exist, so we skip these steps here.

## 3. Field-test design

Before calibration data exist, `design_field_test()` plans the field test:
how many forms, which anchor items they share, and how many candidates each
form needs. It then simulates parameter recovery under that plan.

```{r}
p <- design_field_test(p, n_forms = 2, n_per_form = 600, items = 32,
                       reps = 2, seed = 1)
p$field_test$recovery
flags(p, stage = "field_test")
```

Two forms of 600 candidates recover the slopes with an RMSE a little above
the 0.2 target. The usual answer is more candidates per form. Here we accept
the plan and record why:

```{r}
p <- acknowledge(p, check = "recovery", note = "Sample fixed by the testing window")
```

## 4. Data intake

`add_responses()` scores the raw answers with the key, then checks for
missing data, possible miskeys, straight-lining, rapid guessing and sparse
score categories.

```{r}
p <- add_responses(p, certexam, items = 3:34, key = certexam_key,
                   id = "id", group = "language")
flags(p, stage = "intake")
```

Q14 is answered correctly by almost nobody and has a negative item-total
correlation, which is the signature of a miskey. That is a block flag. Once
the item writer confirms the key was wrong, we drop the item, which marks its
flag as fixed:

```{r}
p <- drop_items(p, "Q14", note = "Key confirmed wrong by the item writer")
```

## 5. Calibration

```{r}
p <- calibrate(p, model = "2PL")
flags(p, stage = "calibration")
```

The calibration gate checks convergence, model fit, local dependence, item
fit, parameter ranges, DIF between the language groups, reliability and
person fit. It finds three planted problems:

- Q21 and Q22 are locally dependent.
- Q09 has large DIF (block).
- Q27 has moderate DIF.

It also reports that reliability falls short of the 0.85 target from the
blueprint. Each needs a decision:

```{r}
p <- acknowledge(p, check = "local_dependence",
                 note = "Q21 and Q22 share a case; keep them apart on forms")
p <- override(p, check = "dif_large", note = "Translation reviewed; French version revised")
p <- acknowledge(p, check = "dif_moderate", note = "Sent to the bias panel")
p <- acknowledge(p, check = "low_reliability",
                 note = "Operational forms will be longer than the field test")
```

`override()` needs a written reason; `acknowledge()` takes an optional note.
Every decision is logged and printed in the report. Run `flags(p, status =
"all")` to see decided flags too.

## 6. The item bank

`bank_items()` stores the calibrated items in an item bank. In a later
administration, `link_to_bank()` puts a new calibration on the bank's scale
through anchor items and checks the anchors for drift.

```{r}
p <- bank_items(p, name = "Certification bank")
p$bank
```

## 7. Forms, adaptive and multistage tests

`assemble_forms()` builds parallel fixed forms with automated test assembly
(through eatATA), meeting a content blueprint and keeping enemy items apart.
`simulate_cat()` and `assemble_mst()` simulate adaptive and multistage tests
with mirtCAT.

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("eatATA", quietly = TRUE)}
content <- setNames(rep(c("Ethics", "Practice", "Law"), c(10, 12, 10)),
                    sprintf("Q%02d", 1:32))
p <- assemble_forms(p, length = 12, n_forms = 2, theta = c(-1, 0, 1),
                    content = content[names(content) != "Q14"],
                    blueprint = c(Ethics = 4, Practice = 5, Law = 3),
                    enemies = list(c("Q21", "Q22")))
p$forms$info
```

The two forms meet the blueprint, keep Q21 and Q22 apart and are parallel:
their information differs by less than 10% at each ability level. The forms
gate also checks measurement precision:

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("eatATA", quietly = TRUE)}
flags(p, stage = "forms")[, c("check", "target", "value", "rule")]
```

Twelve items cannot reach a standard error of 0.35. For a pass/fail decision,
precision matters most near the cut score, which the next stage checks.

## 8. Cut scores

`set_cuts()` takes cut scores on the ability or raw-score scale (or a
standard-setting panel's ratings) and estimates classification accuracy and
consistency.

```{r}
p <- set_cuts(p, cuts = 18, scale = "raw", labels = c("Fail", "Pass"))
p$cuts$summary
flags(p, stage = "cuts")[, c("check", "target", "value", "rule")]
```

Accuracy (0.86) and consistency (0.81) meet the defaults of 0.85 and 0.80,
but the standard error at the cut is above 0.35. More items near the cut
would help, which is the same message the reliability flag gave.

## 9. Scoring

`score_persons()` estimates each candidate's ability and flags imprecise and
extreme scores. Open-ended responses are scored first with `score_open()`,
either by a language model against the item rubrics or by a trained model you
supply. The scores are checked against human scores (quadratic weighted
kappa, standardized mean differences overall and by group).

```{r}
p <- score_persons(p)
head(p$scores)
```

## 10. Test security

`check_security()` looks for evidence that a score may not reflect the
candidate's own ability:

- preknowledge of items suspected to have leaked;
- items leaking across administration windows;
- parameter drift from the bank;
- answer copying;
- aberrant response times;
- sites with too many flagged candidates;
- unusual score gains.

```{r}
p <- check_security(p, leaked = c("Q01", "Q02", "Q03", "Q04", "Q05"))
flags(p, stage = "security")
```

Here no candidate shows evidence of preknowledge of those five items.
Security flags are evidence for an investigation, not proof of misconduct.
The candidates involved are kept in `p$security$persons` for investigators.
Flags and reports give counts only.

## 11. The report

`pipeline_report()` writes an HTML technical report that covers:

- the model and the item statistics;
- a section for each stage that ran;
- every flag and every decision recorded about it;
- the R code that reproduces the pipeline.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
pipeline_report(p, file = "certification-report.html")
```

The code is also in `p$code`:

```{r}
cat(p$code, sep = "\n")
```

## 12. Bank monitoring

After each administration, `monitor_bank()` records it in the bank under a
window name, then checks the bank's history:

- items over-exposed in consecutive windows;
- content cells with too few active items;
- reliability falling from its first value;
- items unused for a year.

```{r}
p <- monitor_bank(p, window = "2026 spring", date = "2026-04-15",
                  content = content)
p$monitoring$windows
p$monitoring$cells
```

The cell minimums come from the blueprint: by default the bank should hold at
least `cell_depth` (2) times each cell's count on a form. Items that a check
flags can be retired or sent back to review with `retire_items()`; they stay
in the bank with their history but are no longer used for forms or linking.

```{r}
p <- retire_items(p, c("Q01", "Q02", "Q03", "Q04", "Q05"),
                  note = "Posted on a study forum; retired as a precaution")
p <- monitor_bank(p, record = FALSE)
flags(p, stage = "monitoring")
```

Retiring five Ethics items leaves that cell with fewer active items than the
blueprint needs, so the next round of item writing should start there.
Retiring items also marks the forms as needing a rerun.
Save the bank with `saveRDS(p$bank, "bank.rds")` to keep its history for the
next administration.

## Where everything stands

Printing the pipeline shows each stage, its summary and its open flags:

```{r}
p
```

## Strict mode and the workbench

For operational work, start the pipeline with `strict = TRUE`. Then a stage
will not run while an earlier stage has open review or block flags, so no
problem can be passed over without a recorded decision.

The **Pipeline** tab of `launch_workbench()` runs uploaded data through the
intake and calibration gates, or loads a pipeline saved with `saveRDS()`. It
shows the stage tracker and the flags. Select flags there to acknowledge,
override or drop items, then recalibrate. The tab shows the R code for every
step as you go.
